literal: Yuwen Heituo killed the Deposed Emperor, and Baoju thereupon usurped the great title.
idiomatic: Yuwen Heituo slew the Deposed Emperor; Yuan Baoju then seized the imperial title.

literal: Prince Qinghe Yi, courtesy name Xuanren.
idiomatic: Qinghe Wang Yi, styled Xuanren.

literal: In youth he was clever and quick-witted, of fine appearance; Emperor Gaozu loved him.
idiomatic: As a boy he was clever and handsome, and Gaozu doted on him.

literal: Prince Pengcheng Xie greatly prized and singled him out, and together they said: "This boy's spirit and bearing are outwardly grand, his yellow core inwardly lustrous; if Heaven grants him years, he will rival the Two Souths.
idiomatic: Prince Pengcheng Xie prized him highly and said with others, "This child's bearing is outwardly grand and inwardly rich; given a full span of years he would rival the Two Souths."

literal: " He ranged broadly through the classics and histories, took in many schools of thought, had literary talent, was skilled at discourse on principle, generous and tolerant in bearing, and did not let joy or anger show on his face.
idiomatic: He mastered classics and histories, absorbed many traditions, wrote well, argued ably, and was magnanimous—joy and anger never showed on his face.

literal: In the twenty-first year of Taihe he was enfeoffed.
idiomatic: He received his fief in Taihe year 21.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Shizong's reign he was appointed Palace Attendant, then transferred to Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: When Shizong acceded he became palace attendant, then vice director of the masters of writing.

literal: Yi was talented and long in government; clear in judgment and decision, he sliced through the multitude of affairs and won a great reputation.
idiomatic: Yi excelled in administration, decided cases with clarity, cut through piled business, and won wide renown.

literal: Minister of Works Gao Zhao, favored as the emperor's maternal uncle, already monopolized awesome power and plotted to remove worthy clansmen, repeatedly slandering Yi and Yu and the rest.
idiomatic: Gao Zhao, the emperor's uncle by marriage, already held unchecked power and sought to purge the princes, repeatedly denouncing Yi, Yu, and others.

literal: Yu could not bear his fury and thereupon raised rebellion in Jizhou.
idiomatic: Yu, unable to endure the pressure, rebelled in Jizhou.

literal: Using Yu's rebellion as pretext, he also framed and killed Xie.
idiomatic: He used Yu's revolt as pretext to frame and kill Xie as well.

literal: Yi feared he could not escape.
idiomatic: Yi feared he would not escape.

literal: Zhao again reviewed prisoners to build private goodwill.
idiomatic: Zhao again reviewed prisoners to curry private favor.

literal: At a banquet where Yi attended him, wine deep, Yi said to Zhao: "The Son of Heaven's brothers—how many are there?—yet you blaze on without cease.
idiomatic: When wine had deepened at a feast Yi told Zhao, "The emperor's brothers are few—why does your flame never die down?"

literal: In old times Wang Mang's head was bald, yet he still relied on kin through the empress's family and usurped the Han house; now your bent form is already plain to see—I fear you will again become the stairway of disorder.
idiomatic: Wang Mang was bald yet rode empress-kin ties to seize the Han throne; your crooked shape is plain already—I fear you will be disorder's stair again."

literal: " He also said to Emperor Shizong: "Your servant has heard that vessels and names may not be lent to others.
idiomatic: He also told Shizong, "I have heard that ritual vessels and titles must not be lent away."

literal: Therefore when the Ji clan overstepped at Mount Tai, Confucius deeply censured it;
idiomatic: When the Ji clan overreached at Mount Tai, Confucius censured it deeply;

literal: when Zhongsun hung his drums as for a lord, Qiu Ming took it as the utmost warning.
idiomatic: when Zhongsun's house displayed lordly drums, Qiu Ming called it the gravest warning.

literal: Truly heaven is honored and earth is lowly—the way of ruler and minister is distinct; one should stop the first sprout and guard against encroachment.
idiomatic: Heaven is high and earth low; ruler and minister are separate—one must nip usurpation in the bud.

literal: As for reducing meals and reviewing prisoners—these are a ruler's affairs; now the Minister of Works performs them—how is that the meaning of a subject?
idiomatic: Reducing meals and reviewing prisoners belong to the ruler; for the minister of works to do them—what subject's duty is that?

literal: Moreover Your Majesty reforms government and teaching and releases prisoners from litigation—then timely rain may descend and the jade candle know harmony; why let an enlightened ruler lose them above while treacherous ministers steal them below?
idiomatic: If Your Majesty reforms rule and clears suits, timely rain and harmony follow—why let the wise ruler lose these above while traitors seize them below?

literal: The root of long disorder lies here.
idiomatic: The root of lasting disorder is here."

literal: " Emperor Shizong smiled and did not answer.
idiomatic: Shizong smiled and made no reply.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Suzong's reign he was transferred to Grand Marshal, Palace Attendant as before.
idiomatic: At Suzong's accession he was made grand marshal while remaining palace attendant.

literal: An edict ordered Yi to decide affairs of the Gate and Chamber.
idiomatic: An edict put Gate-and-Chamber business in Yi's hands.

literal: He also oversaw annotated classics.
idiomatic: He also directed classical annotation.

literal: At the time there was a monk named Huilian who claimed that charmed water given to drink could cure all illnesses.
idiomatic: A monk Huilian claimed his charmed water cured every illness.

literal: Those who came to him sick numbered thousands a day.
idiomatic: Sick people flocked to him by the thousand each day.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling ordered food and clothing supplied, with support unusually heavy, and had him treat the people's illnesses south of the western city.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Ling fed and clothed him lavishly and set him to treat commoners' illnesses south of the western city.

literal: Yi memorialized in remonstrance: "Your servant has heard that the law deeply punishes deluding the masses and the rites utterly forbid demonic lewdness—all to make dwelling in the upright bright and to dam and block wickedness.
idiomatic: Yi remonstrated: "Law punishes deluding the people; rites forbid demonic excess—all to keep the throne upright and bar wickedness."

literal: In old times at the end of Han there was Zhang Jiao, who also used this art to dazzle and bewitch the age.
idiomatic: At Han's end Zhang Jiao had used the same art to bewitch his age.

literal: Considering what he did, it does not differ from today.
idiomatic: His methods differ in no way from today's.

literal: He could thereby seduce living men and bring the calamity of the Yellow Scarves; for decades the realm was scorched—that was Jiao's doing.
idiomatic: He seduced the living and brought the Yellow Scarves; for decades the realm burned—that was Jiao.

literal: In old times the adulterer Xinyuan did not ascend the Bright Hall;
idiomatic: Of old the adulterer Xinyuan never reached the Bright Hall;

literal: Wuli the opportunist in the end suffered the manifest execution.
idiomatic: Wuli the opportunist died by public execution.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling, because Yi was Suzong's honored younger uncle and his virtue was foremost before all eyes, entrusted him with court government, his affairs modeled on the Duke of Zhou and Huo.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Ling, seeing Yi as Xiaoming's honored uncle and a man all eyes followed, entrusted government to him on the model of Zhou Gong and Huo Qubing.

literal: Yi strove with all his strength to support and correct, taking the realm as his own charge.
idiomatic: Yi labored to steady the state and took the realm as his charge.

literal: Commander of the Guards Yuan Cha, the empress dowager's sister's husband, relied on favor and was arrogant to excess.
idiomatic: Yuan Cha, the dowager's brother-in-law and commander of the guards, grew insolent on favor.

literal: Yi restrained him by law and each time demoted and disgraced him; Cha therefore hated him.
idiomatic: Yi checked him with law and repeatedly humiliated him; Cha came to hate him.

literal: A partisan of Cha, Direct-Gate Gentleman Song Wei, pleased to Cha's intent, [7] reported that Yi plotted rebellion; they sealed Yi's Gate and Chamber staff, questioned his attendants and court nobles—the noble accounts were clear, and he was only then cleared and released.
idiomatic: Cha's man Song Wei, eager to please, [7] accused Yi of treason; they sealed his staff and questioned attendants and nobles until the truth cleared him.

literal: Yi, loyal yet slandered, thereupon gathered former loyal and fierce men and made Records of Manifest Loyalty in twenty scrolls to show his intent.
idiomatic: Slandered though loyal, Yi compiled Records of Manifest Loyalty in twenty scrolls to declare his mind.

literal: In the seventh month of the first year of Zhenguang, Cha with Liu Teng forced Emperor Suzong in Xianyang Hall, shut Empress Dowager Ling in the rear palace, imprisoned Yi in the Gate and Chamber office, fabricated Yi's crimes, and killed him; he was thirty-four.
idiomatic: In Zhenguang year 1, seventh month, Cha and Liu Teng seized Xiaoming in Xianyang Hall, walled the dowager in the rear palace, jailed Yi in the Gate and Chamber office, forged charges, and killed him at thirty-four.

literal: Court and countryside, noble and common, whether they knew him or not, held grief and lost breath; shock rolled through far and near.
idiomatic: Court and countryside, knowing him or not, grieved until breath failed; shock rolled far and near.

literal: Barbarians in the capital and those who had returned, hearing of Yi's death, split their faces in mourning—several hundred men.
idiomatic: Barbarians in the capital and those returned, hearing of his death, lacerated their faces in mourning—several hundred men.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: Prince Guangping Huai.
idiomatic: Guangping Wang Huai.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: There were princes of Wei.
idiomatic: Among the princes of Wei,

literal: They were summoned into the separate lodge of the Hualin Park, their going out and coming in forbidden, and Four-Gate Academician Dong Zheng was ordered to teach them the classics and transmissions.
idiomatic: they were summoned to the Hualin Park lodge, confined from going abroad, and Four-Gate academician Dong Zheng taught them the classics.

literal: When Emperor Shizong died they were then able to return.
idiomatic: When Shizong died they were allowed home.

literal: Prince Runan Yue loved reading Buddhist sutras and perusing books and histories.
idiomatic: Runan Wang Yue loved Buddhist sutras and historical books.

literal: By nature he was unorthodox, untrammeled and hard to fathom.
idiomatic: His nature was erratic, rakish, and unpredictable.

literal: Yue's consort, Lady Lu of the Eastern Sea duke's house, bore one son but received no courteous treatment.
idiomatic: His consort Lady Lu, daughter of the Eastern Sea duke, bore a son yet won no courtesy.

literal: There was Cui Yanxia, who by heterodox ways kept company with Yue and together took elixir medicines of pine and zhuyu and the like.
idiomatic: Cui Yanxia, a man of left-hand ways, joined Yue in taking immortality drugs of pine and atractylodes.

literal: At times he went out lightly to gather fungus and lodged in commoners' dwellings outside the walls.
idiomatic: He would slip out to gather fungi and sleep in hovels outside the walls.

literal: He then cut off wine, meat, millet, and rice and ate only wheat porridge.
idiomatic: He renounced wine, meat, millet, and rice and ate only wheat gruel.

literal: He also ceased the bedchamber and came to prefer male beauty.
idiomatic: He abandoned the bedchamber and favored men instead.

literal: In his temper he resented consorts and concubines, even beating them, treating them like maidservants.
idiomatic: He resented his women, beat them like servants, and treated them as maids.

literal: When Yue went out his consort lodged in a separate residence.
idiomatic: When Yue traveled his consort stayed in a separate house.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling ordered an inquiry; she was brought in and Yue's conduct was exhaustively examined.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Ling ordered an inquiry; the consort was brought in and Yue's conduct fully examined.

literal: The consort, sick from the cane, lay prostrate on the bed mat; her sores were not yet healed.
idiomatic: The consort, flogged sick, lay on her mat; the wounds had not healed.

literal: Because Yue had caned the consort, the empress dowager thereupon ordered the practice forbidden.
idiomatic: Because Yue had beaten her, the dowager forbade such abuse.

literal: She ordered all imperial princes and the three frontier princedoms that if a principal consort was ill more than a hundred days, all were to memorialize and report.
idiomatic: She ordered every imperial prince and frontier prince: if a principal consort was ill beyond a hundred days, they must report it.

literal: If any still applied the cane, their fief and rank were to be stripped on the spot.
idiomatic: Anyone who still beat her would lose fief and rank at once.

literal: When Qinghe Wang Yi was killed by Yuan Cha, Yue had not the slightest thought of vengeance; he waited on him with mulberry-fall wine and exhausted private flattery.
idiomatic: When Qinghe Wang Yi fell to Yuan Cha, Yue bore no grudge; he courted Cha with mulberry-fall wine and shameless flattery.

literal: Cha was greatly pleased and made Yue Palace Attendant and Grand Marshal.
idiomatic: Cha was delighted and made him palace attendant and grand marshal.

literal: On the day of his investiture he went to Yi's son Chan to request Yi's robes and curios; Chan did not promptly please him.
idiomatic: On the day of appointment he asked Yi's son Chan for his father's robes and curios; Chan displeased him.

literal: He thereupon summoned Chan and caned him a hundred strokes.
idiomatic: He summoned Chan and beat him a hundred strokes.

literal: Chan was in mourning hut, the burial not yet performed; his form and breath were frail and weak—suddenly subjected to fierce blows, he nearly did not survive.
idiomatic: Chan still mourned unburied, frail in body—sudden blows nearly killed him.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: He still called "Little son" and personally stroked and comforted him.
idiomatic: He still called "Little son" and comforted him with his own hands.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: Yue set a great mortar-pestle at the province gate; [9] for thieves he would at once wish to cut off their hands.
idiomatic: Yue placed a great crushing mortar at the province gate; [9] thieves he would have their hands cut off at once.

literal: People at the time feared his unpredictability and that he could perform strange deeds; thieves and rogues feared him and for a time ceased.
idiomatic: People feared his whims and strange punishments; theft briefly ceased.

literal: When Erzhu Rong raised troops toward Luoyang.
idiomatic: When Erzhu Rong marched on Luoyang,

literal: Already he recalled entering among men.
idiomatic: The text is corrupt; he may already have hoped to enter Luoyang.

literal: The reading here is doubtful.
idiomatic: 〈Doubtful text; the transmitted line is corrupt.〉

literal: Before long he heard that Rong had wantonly slaughtered at Heyin and thereupon fled south to Xiao Yan.
idiomatic: Soon he heard Rong's massacre at Heyin and fled south to Xiao Yan.

literal: Yan installed him as Wei sovereign and changed the reign title to Gengxing.
idiomatic: Xiao Yan set him up as Wei ruler under the reign title Gengxing.

literal: Yan sent his general Wang Bian to escort and place him on the border; [10] thereby to covet invasion and pressure.
idiomatic: Xiao Yan sent Wang Bian to place him on the border [10] as a lever for invasion.

literal: When Duke Xianwu of Qi had already killed Rong, because Yue was Emperor Gaozu's son and ought to inherit the great enterprise, he therefore had someone convey his intent.
idiomatic: After Duke Xianwu of Qi killed Rong, deeming Yue Gaozu's son fit for the throne, he sent word of his intent.

literal: Yue, having arrived, was wild and unbridled as before; his actions were crimes and failures—he could not be supported, and they stopped.
idiomatic: Yue arrived as reckless as ever; his acts were crimes—he could not be enthroned, and they desisted.

literal: At the beginning of the Deposed Emperor's reign he was appointed Grand Marshal.
idiomatic: At the Deposed Emperor's accession he was made grand marshal.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died in office.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: In the tables of contents of all editions of Wei shu juan 22 this scroll is marked as lacunose.
idiomatic: Every edition's table of contents marks Wei shu juan 22 as lacunose.

literal: After the scroll there should have been Song-dynasty collation notes; transmitted copies have lost them.
idiomatic: Song collation notes after the scroll are missing from transmitted copies.

literal: The Palace Edition textual verification states: "Wei Shou's book is lacunose; later men supplemented it.
idiomatic: The Palace Edition notes: "Wei Shou's text is missing; later hands supplied this."

literal: " On examination the transmitted text too was supplemented from Beishi juan 19, Biographies of Xiaowen's Five Princes, with overflowing words and phrases that should come from the Minor History of the Gao clan.
idiomatic: " The received text, save stray phrases, was patched from Beishi juan 19 (Xiaowen's Five Princes); overflow wording likely comes from the Gao clan Minor History.

literal: The Beishi Five Princes biography is also defective—for example the biography of Guangping Wang Huai survives in only thirty-five characters, and the biography of Runan Wang Yue also has much missing text; this biography is the same.
idiomatic: Beishi's Five Princes lives are also broken: Guangping Wang Huai's survives in thirty-five characters, Runan Wang Yue's is heavily lacunose—this life matches.

literal: Guangping Wenmu Wang Huai: juan 11 of the Annals of the Deposed Emperor reads "Guangping Wumu Wang."
idiomatic: Guangping Wenmu Wang Huai: juan 11 of the Deposed Emperor's annals reads "Guangping Wumu Wang."

literal: Collected Epitaphs and Interpretations: epitaph of Yuan Huai
idiomatic: Collected Epitaphs: epitaph of Yuan Huai

literal: 〈Plate 193〉
idiomatic: (Plate 193)

literal: It states "posthumous title Wumu."
idiomatic: It gives the posthumous title Wumu.

literal: Collected Interpretations juan 4 cites Yuan Ti
idiomatic: Collected Interpretations, juan 4, draws on Yuan Ti

literal: 〈Plate 194〉
idiomatic: (Plate 194)

literal: , and Yuan Hui
idiomatic: and Yuan Hui
